nice what does this say about it

The article says the 2026 Zeekr 7X Performance AWD is a bloody impressive electric SUV from China that’s making waves in Australia. It’s the top-selling medium SUV over $60k and third-best EV overall here. The dual motor AWD version packs 475kW and 710Nm, with a 100kWh battery giving 543km range. Charging is a ripper too, with up to 296kW DC charging speed.

It’s got fancy gear like 21-inch forged wheels, adaptive suspension, Nappa leather, 21-speaker audio, massive infotainment screens, and a 36-inch head-up display. Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, and wireless chargers are there, but phones get hot charging.

The power doors are a pain, requiring a button push and often not opening fully — a design fail. Inside, it’s a comfy, well-built ride that’s not too techy or minimalist. The drive is solid, quick enough to smoke smaller petrol SUVs but not a supercar rocket. It’s heavy but handles well for a big SUV.

Rear passengers get space and recline seats, but no spare tyre is a bummer. Overall, it’s a great family EV with heaps of gear and decent price, rivaling Tesla Model Y and XPeng G6.

Score: 4.5/5 — pretty damn good!

can you give me the main specs on this beast

Sure thing, here’s the gist of the 2026 Zeekr 7X specs from that review:

- Battery: 100 kWh CATL “Kettle” battery pack, 800V architecture  
- Motor: Single electric motor on rear axle (Long Range RWD), 300 kW power  
- Range: Claimed over 600 km (real world around 500+ km at 110 km/h)  
- Charging: Up to 420 kW DC fast charging capability (but Aussie max ~350 kW available)  
- AC Charging: 22 kW onboard charger  
- Drive: Rear Wheel Drive (long range model), AWD on higher trims  
- Performance AWD Model: 475 kW and 710 Nm (dual motor)  
- Wheels: 21-inch forged wheels on performance model  
- Suspension: Adaptive on performance model, standard on others  
- Interior: Synthetic leather (polyurethane coated fabric), 14-way power seats with heating, cooling, massage  
- Infotainment: 16.3" touchscreen, Qualcomm Snapdragon processor, Android Auto & Apple CarPlay (wired/wireless)  
- Audio: 21-speaker system (used to be Yamaha, now Zeekr branded)  
- Safety: 7 airbags, 5-star Euro NCAP rating, not yet tested by Aussie safety authority  
- Dimensions: Just under 4.8m length, roomy interior for size  
- Features: 36-inch head-up display, 13-inch digital instrument cluster, multiple driving modes, power tailgate, V2L (3.3 kW) and V2G (future, warranty void if used)  
- Price: Starts just under $58k AUD for base RWD, mid-spec long range around $64k AUD driveaway  

This thing is a solid premium electric SUV with great range, fast charging, and plenty of tech and comfort for Aussie families.

Want the juicy bits on driving experience or interior?
sure

Alright, here’s the lowdown on driving and interior from the review:

**Driving Experience:**
- Smooth, solid, and responsive without being scary.
- Rear-wheel drive setup gives it a nice glide and good grip.
- Steering wheel has a quirky “squirl” shape, but feels great and gives more grip for tight turns.
- Handles city and twisty roads well, though not quite as sharp as a Tesla Model Y or German luxury SUVs.
- Autonomous driving tech is pretty good, mostly handles lane keeping and cruise control well.
- Ride comfort is impressive even without air suspension on the tested model.
- Acceleration from the single rear motor is decent at 300 kW, with even more powerful variants available in China.
- Quiet cabin with minimal tyre and wind noise.

**Interior:**
- Feels way more expensive than the price suggests.
- Clean, tidy design with minimal buttons, good for OCD types.
- Synthetic leather (PU coated fabric) seats are comfy, supportive, and have heating, cooling, and massage.
- Front seats have 14-way power adjustment.
- Rear seats are roomy with great legroom, recline, and amenities like air vents, USB-C ports, and reading lights.
- 21-speaker audio system is rich and sharp.
- Huge 16-inch infotainment screen runs smoothly with Snapdragon processor.
- Wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay work well, but phones tend to get hot while charging.
- Some annoying quirks like power doors that sometimes don’t open properly and fiddly touchscreen controls for mirrors and air vents.
- Good storage options and secret cubbies around the cabin.
- No in-vehicle fridge unlike some Chinese rivals.

Overall, it nails premium feel and comfort without going overboard on unnecessary tech gimmicks. Pretty bloody impressive for under 65 grand driveaway.
